drafts.title: Hypothetical: 18 vs 24 t/s - What's Missing from Local LLM Benchmarks?
drafts.body: This is a hypothetical exploration based on synthetic data, not personal experience. We're considering two hypothetical local inference runtimes achieving 18 and 24 tokens per second (t/s) on the same hardware with a single, identical prompt [F1]. While a higher t/s number like 24 t/s appears superior to 18 t/s, this specific hypothetical test setup has significant limitations [F2]. Crucially, factors vital for user experience, such as the time to the first token (TTFT) and the actual quality of the generated answers, were not assessed in this scenario [F3]. A model that generates tokens faster might still feel unresponsive if it takes a long time to start generating. Similarly, rapid output is less valuable if the content is inaccurate or nonsensical. This limited data point does not establish a definitive winner for all use cases [F4]. What other metrics beyond raw t/s do you find critical for evaluating local LLM performance in practice?
drafts.plan: Introduce the hypothetical t/s values and immediately pivot to the limitations of such metrics. Explain that TTFT and answer quality were not part of the hypothetical test. State that this doesn't represent a universal conclusion and ask the community about other important performance factors they consider.

drafts.title: Hypothetical Local LLM Performance: Beyond Raw Token Speed
drafts.body: We're examining a hypothetical scenario where two local LLM configurations yield 18 and 24 tokens per second (t/s) respectively [F1]. This comparison was conducted on identical hardware using a single prompt [F2]. While the 24 t/s result is numerically higher, it's essential to understand what this hypothetical metric *doesn't* tell us. The hypothetical experiment did not capture the time taken to generate the first token, nor did it evaluate the quality or coherence of the model's output [F3]. A faster raw token rate could be misleading if the initial response latency is high or if the generated text requires substantial editing. Therefore, this specific hypothetical comparison cannot be generalized as a definitive performance benchmark for all situations or models [F4]. What aspects of inference speed, beyond tokens per second, are most important for your local LLM usage?
drafts.plan: Present the hypothetical token speeds and the controlled test conditions. Clearly state the missing metrics (TTFT, quality) and their importance. Emphasize that this hypothetical result is not a universal indicator and solicit community input on alternative performance considerations.

drafts.title: Hypothetical Token/Second Rates: A Limited View of Local LLM Speed
drafts.body: Consider a hypothetical benchmark where two setups achieve 18 t/s and 24 t/s respectively [F1]. This test was run on the same machine with a single prompt, providing a controlled, albeit narrow, comparison [F2]. While the difference in tokens per second is clear, this hypothetical data is incomplete. It omits critical usability factors: the time until the first token appears (TTFT) and the qualitative assessment of the generated response [F3]. A model might achieve a high t/s rate but feel slow if it has a long TTFT. Conversely, rapid output of low-quality text is not ideal. Consequently, we cannot conclude that one hypothetical runtime is universally superior based solely on these figures [F4]. What other factors, besides raw t/s, influence your perception of a local LLM's responsiveness and utility?
drafts.plan: Introduce the hypothetical t/s figures and the controlled testing environment. Explicitly mention the missing metrics (TTFT, output quality) and explain why they matter. State that the hypothetical results do not generalize and ask the community to share other relevant performance indicators they prioritize.
